On May 6, 2013, at 8:02 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

I found an issue:

the initial value isn't passed to sampler.init_stepsize() (base_hmc). So, the q value of _z is always 0 to start. The p is sampled properly. Michael, what's the best way of passing that into the sampler? seed()?



On Mon, May 6, 2013 at 1:49 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
Right, in general they will be different.  If they are the same and the metrics are the same (unlikely since they are factored differently) then the results will still be slightly different due to the jitter, but you can suppress that with --epsilon_pm=0 on both versions.  If you want to focus on the stepsize adaptation then just use --equal_step_sizes

On May 6, 2013, at 6:35 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

Ok, so the epsilons shouldn't match then. (Let me know if that's correct.)

If we're past this step and the epsilons do match, should we be expecting identical results?


On Mon, May 6, 2013 at 1:32 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
No, they shouldn't match.  For some reason Matt used the log prob when determining the HMC acceptance rate here, which is not the best way to determine the optimal HMC stepsize.  The new implementation uses the full Hamiltonian, which is correct.

On May 6, 2013, at 6:27 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

In init_stepsize() in base_hmc, should:

        double delta_H = H0 - this->_hamiltonian.H(this->_z);
        int direction = delta_H > log(0.5) ? 1 : -1;

match:

        double H = logp - lastlogp;
        int direction = H > log(0.5) ? 1 : -1;

from find_reasonable_parameters() in hmc_base.hpp?

Right now, delta_H in the new code is:
H0: 1.257892961
H:  1.257924408
delta_H: -3.144732402e-05

where as in the old code:
lastlogp: -1.99975
logp: -0.171807
H: 1.82794

These are with the same seeds, same init values, etc.


On Mon, May 6, 2013 at 1:14 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
So, before we get into improving performance, I'm more concerned that we can't replicate things between mac/windows AND current behavior is different from the past.


On Mon, May 6, 2013 at 1:12 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
Before we get to dual-averaging, I'm seeing differences in:
v1.3.0: find_reasonable_parameters()
master: init_stepsize()

For the simple normal(0,1) model (src/models/command.stan), I'm seeing an epsilon for v1.3.0 at 2 and a nom_epsilon for master at 3.2.

Are these supposed to behave identically?


On Mon, May 6, 2013 at 1:09 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
In what sense? The additional step size adaptation window should significantly improve performance - is it massively better?

My Internet situation is sketchy right now but I can correspond via email.  

On May 6, 2013, at 5:33 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

Michael,

I'm seeing some massive differences in the implementation of the dual-averaging. This could be the cause of some of our problems. Let me know when you want to talk through it.


Daniel

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
parts: > Is jittering turned on by default? If so, why?
Defaults to zero jitter, just as before.

> What exactly are you passing to the step size adaptation to tell it
> whether the step size is too small or too large?
The average acceptance probability of the tree, just as before.

> How are you deciding whether to use a sample from the new half-tree or
> the old half-tree?
Uniformly based on total valid points in the subtree, just as before.

> I'm concerned that the "refactor" has made some significant changes to
> the actual algorithm, and that these changes haven't been adequately
> tested.

I may very well have made an error somewhere, but every attempt was made to reproduce the old algorithm exactly unless I found an explicit error (as in the stepsize initialization - I can't recall another instance).  In particular I did a bunch of tests on the interaction between stepsize and tree structure and everything behaved as expected.

parts: Sure, but we don't normally use that state outside of actual sampling because it was decided that the sampler would only transform an input sample and not carry the state of the Markov chain internally (technically the state is stored, but it's always overwritten). Having adaptation really motivates the other approach, where the constructor you note would be much more natural.

parts:
Ok, I'll take a closer look at the code and double-check. I got a
little confused by the util.sum_prob, but now I see that it's not
being used to decide which branch to sample from but only as a measure
of integrator accuracy. One minor difference, though, is that in the
old version we only computed the average probability for the most
recent half of the tree, excluding the states in the half-tree nearest
the starting point. This is because the first state is always
acceptable, so including states near the start state biases our
estimate of the average acceptance probability upwards (though
probably only slightly). I think the original behavior could be
brought back by moving

util.n_tree = 0;
util.sum_prob = 0;

into the while loop.

BTW, can someone remind me how to set off code so that it looks nice
in these emails? Ben's code snippets always look so much nicer than
mine...

Matt

parts:
So....I may have been premature.  I found two somewhat serious bugs in the NUTS code -- it's amazing they didn't manifest as more serious sampling problems (and frustrating, because I had extensively checked for those kinds of problems when first writing up the new code -- I have no idea what happened in between).  It seemed like the errors were introducing larger gradients which allowed very small differences in floating point calculations to leak into the sampler, accumulate, and eventually become nontrivial.  But even after fixing those problems and verifying that NUTS behaves as expected, Mac/Windows are different.  I'm still neck deep in code, hopefully something will turn up.

Incidentally, I can at least explain why the Mac/Windows code seems to "diverge".  The numerical differences eventually affect the NUTS criterion, and at a given iteration the tree on one machine reaches a deeper depth than on the other.  This misaligns the random number generators and the resulting sequence of samples.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
parts:
I'm not sure it's worth looking too closely for the Mac/Windows discrepancy.

There are a number of reasons that different compilers/optimization
levels/CPUs/platforms/etc would give slightly different floating point
results. E.G., is one using x87 instructions while another is using
SSE instructions at some point? With x87 instructions, some floating
point ops are done at 80bit (long double) precision and the result
gets truncated down to 64bit when they're written to memory or
registers. This can result in slightly different results on different
platforms. Unfortunately, there's not too much we can do about that.

Cheers,
Marcus

parts:
We're actually trying to understand the fundamental differences in code from v1.3.0 and current master. This is manifesting itself as differences in Mac/Windows right now. There's something else going on and if we knew what it was, we'd be ok with it.

We're not actually too concerned with floating point differences. Now, with that said, we can't draw the same first sample in Mac and Windows in master, which we were able to do in v1.3.0. We should either be able to reproduce that behavior or explain why we have differences.

On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 3:00 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
I'm not sure it's worth looking too closely for the Mac/Windows discrepancy.

There are a number of reasons that different compilers/optimization
levels/CPUs/platforms/etc would give slightly different floating point
results.  E.G., is one using x87 instructions while another is using
SSE instructions at some point?  With x87 instructions, some floating
point ops are done at 80bit (long double) precision and the result
gets truncated down to 64bit when they're written to memory or
registers.  This can result in slightly different results on different
platforms.  Unfortunately, there's not too much we can do about that.

Cheers,
Marcus

> Ok, I'll take a closer look at the code and double-check. I got a

> being used to decide which branch to sample from but only as a measure
> of integrator accuracy. One minor difference, though, is that in the
> old version we only computed the average probability for the most
> recent half of the tree, excluding the states in the half-tree nearest
> the starting point. This is because the first state is always
> acceptable, so including states near the start state biases our
> estimate of the average acceptance probability upwards (though
> probably only slightly). I think the original behavior could be
> brought back by moving
>
> util.n_tree = 0;
> util.sum_prob = 0;
>
> into the while loop.
>

> mine...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
parts:
I went through all of the code again this morning, focusing on tracing differences between 1.3.0 NUTS and master NUTS. Everything looks to be equivalent except for a small difference in the NUTS criterion that can lead to significant differences (not necessarily errors, just differences) in the resulting trees, and hence samples, when we aggressively push the integrator step size.

If we had a perfect integrator then the two algorithms would be equivalent with

rho (new algorithm) = \delta x (old algorithm) \propto \int dt M^{-1} p(t)

When we appeal to the leapfrog integrator, however, these end up being slightly different,

rho = sum_{i} M^{-1} p^{i}

\delta x = sum_{i} M^{-1} p^{i - 1/2}

i.e. the old algorithm aggregates the momenta at the half step whereas the new algorithm uses the momenta after the full step.

When the accuracy of the integrator is limited by a large step size (which may be totally fine for HMC) this difference can be nontrivial, especially when the tree depth is big. Again, this just explains differences in the exact sequence of samples and possibly different sensitivities to floating point arithmetic; both should yield fine inferences.

-Mike
